journal.book:
MY PLAYBOOK

Why I am doing this
- Being fully present with the people I love
- Clear mornings and steady energy
- Becoming someone I am proud of

My rule
I log slips instead of hiding them. A slip is data, not a reset.

If this, then that
If I am in bed late at night, then Get up and leave the room for 10 minutes. Water, stretch, tidy something. Then back to bed without my phone.
If I am lonely or low, then Text or call one person. A message counts. Or go somewhere with people around.
If I am bored or idle, then 10-minute walk outside, or 10 minutes on a hobby or project.
If I am stressed or anxious, then Move my body (walk, pushups), then write one sentence about what is stressing me.

If I slip
1. Log it in 30 seconds. No hiding.
2. One small action within the hour: water, step outside, or text someone.
3. No big decisions tonight, and no "I blew it" verdicts.
4. Tomorrow: check in as usual. Nothing resets. Ask what the trigger was and what to change.
5. If I want to, tell my safe person: "I slipped."

What I have learned
1. You do not need to feel ready: No. Mixed feelings are a normal part of change. Start with one small step, and let your own reasons carry it.
2. Urges are waves: An urge rises, peaks, and passes. You do not have to fight it or obey it. Notice it, breathe, and outlast this one.
3. Why one slip snowballs: The slip is not the biggest risk. The thought “I blew it, so why bother” is. Protect your confidence and do the next small thing.
4. Late and low: Tired and lonely both make porn look like a bigger reward than it is. Meet the need under the urge: sleep, or a real person.
5. Name the act, not yourself: Describe what you did, not who you are: “I slipped last night,” not “I am a failure.” Then protect your next good move.
6. Kindness after a slip: No. Kindness did not make people give in more. Talk to yourself the way you would to a friend, then do the next small thing.
7. Secrets are heavy: A secret weighs on you every time it comes to mind, not only when you hide it. One safe person can share the weight.
9. If this, then that: Decide ahead of time with an if-then plan: “If this happens, then I will do that.” At 1 AM you only have to follow it.
10. Change the setting: Habits lean on their setting: the room, the device, the hour. Change the setting, and the cue gets weaker.
12. What getting better looks like: Getting better is growth with setbacks, across a whole life: health, home, purpose, and people. A streak is one part, not the whole picture.
13. Name the feeling: Urges often ride in on a feeling. Name it in a word or two, and it loses some of its grip. Then meet that feeling another way.
15. Move your body: Yes. A short burst of movement eases cravings for a while. When an urge starts, move first, then decide.
16. Thoughts are not orders: They are thoughts, not orders. Notice them, name them, and still choose. You do not have to argue with them or obey them.
19. Learn from your own log: Write it down, then look back. Once a week, ask what the log is telling you: when it is hard, what sets it off, and what helps.
20. Fewer fights, not more willpower: Not mostly. People with strong self-control fight temptation less, not more. Arrange your day so the fight happens less, and count the fights you skip.
21. Missing a day: No. A single missed day barely dents a new habit, but misses add up. The day after, come back in the smallest way.
23. Plan the empty hour: Do not wait to feel like it. Put a real, small activity in your hardest hour, and do it even if you do not feel like it.
28. Why groups help: Groups change who you spend time with, and that is one of the main ways they help. Start small: listen at one meeting, or ask one person to check in.

journal.book:
MY PLAYBOOK

Why I am doing this
- Being fully present with the people I love
- Clear mornings and steady energy
- Becoming someone I am proud of

My rule
I log slips instead of hiding them. A slip is data, not a reset.

If this, then that
If I am in bed late at night, then Get up and leave the room for 10 minutes. Water, stretch, tidy something. Then back to bed without my phone.
If I am lonely or low, then Text or call one person. A message counts. Or go somewhere with people around.
If I am bored or idle, then 10-minute walk outside, or 10 minutes on a hobby or project.
If I am stressed or anxious, then Move my body (walk, pushups), then write one sentence about what is stressing me.

If I slip
1. Log it in 30 seconds. No hiding.
2. One small action within the hour: water, step outside, or text someone.
3. No big decisions tonight, and no "I blew it" verdicts.
4. Tomorrow: check in as usual. Nothing resets. Ask what the trigger was and what to change.
5. If I want to, tell my safe person: "I slipped."

What I have learned
1. You do not need to feel ready: No. Mixed feelings are a normal part of change. Start with one small step, and let your own reasons carry it.
2. Urges are waves: An urge rises, peaks, and passes. You do not have to fight it or obey it. Notice it, breathe, and outlast this one.
3. Why one slip snowballs: The slip is not the biggest risk. The thought “I blew it, so why bother” is. Protect your confidence and do the next small thing.
4. Late and low: Tired and lonely both make porn look like a bigger reward than it is. Meet the need under the urge: sleep, or a real person.
5. Name the act, not yourself: Describe what you did, not who you are: “I slipped last night,” not “I am a failure.” Then protect your next good move.
6. Kindness after a slip: No. Kindness did not make people give in more. Talk to yourself the way you would to a friend, then do the next small thing.
7. Secrets are heavy: A secret weighs on you every time it comes to mind, not only when you hide it. One safe person can share the weight.
9. If this, then that: Decide ahead of time with an if-then plan: “If this happens, then I will do that.” At 1 AM you only have to follow it.
10. Change the setting: Habits lean on their setting: the room, the device, the hour. Change the setting, and the cue gets weaker.
12. What getting better looks like: Getting better is growth with setbacks, across a whole life: health, home, purpose, and people. A streak is one part, not the whole picture.
13. Name the feeling: Urges often ride in on a feeling. Name it in a word or two, and it loses some of its grip. Then meet that feeling another way.
15. Move your body: Yes. A short burst of movement eases cravings for a while. When an urge starts, move first, then decide.
16. Thoughts are not orders: They are thoughts, not orders. Notice them, name them, and still choose. You do not have to argue with them or obey them.
19. Learn from your own log: Write it down, then look back. Once a week, ask what the log is telling you: when it is hard, what sets it off, and what helps.
20. Fewer fights, not more willpower: Not mostly. People with strong self-control fight temptation less, not more. Arrange your day so the fight happens less, and count the fights you skip.
21. Missing a day: No. A single missed day barely dents a new habit, but misses add up. The day after, come back in the smallest way.
23. Plan the empty hour: Do not wait to feel like it. Put a real, small activity in your hardest hour, and do it even if you do not feel like it.
28. Why groups help: Groups change who you spend time with, and that is one of the main ways they help. Start small: listen at one meeting, or ask one person to check in.

journal.book:
MY PLAYBOOK

Why I am doing this
- Being fully present with the people I love
- Clear mornings and steady energy
- Becoming someone I am proud of

My rule
I log slips instead of hiding them. A slip is data, not a reset.

If this, then that
If I am in bed late at night, then Get up and leave the room for 10 minutes. Water, stretch, tidy something. Then back to bed without my phone.
If I am lonely or low, then Text or call one person. A message counts. Or go somewhere with people around.
If I am bored or idle, then 10-minute walk outside, or 10 minutes on a hobby or project.
If I am stressed or anxious, then Move my body (walk, pushups), then write one sentence about what is stressing me.

If I slip
1. Log it in 30 seconds. No hiding.
2. One small action within the hour: water, step outside, or text someone.
3. No big decisions tonight, and no "I blew it" verdicts.
4. Tomorrow: check in as usual. Nothing resets. Ask what the trigger was and what to change.
5. If I want to, tell my safe person: "I slipped."

What I have learned
1. You do not need to feel ready: No. Mixed feelings are a normal part of change. Start with one small step, and let your own reasons carry it.
2. Urges are waves: An urge rises, peaks, and passes. You do not have to fight it or obey it. Notice it, breathe, and outlast this one.
3. Why one slip snowballs: The slip is not the biggest risk. The thought “I blew it, so why bother” is. Protect your confidence and do the next small thing.
4. Late and low: Tired and lonely both make porn look like a bigger reward than it is. Meet the need under the urge: sleep, or a real person.
5. Name the act, not yourself: Describe what you did, not who you are: “I slipped last night,” not “I am a failure.” Then protect your next good move.
6. Kindness after a slip: No. Kindness did not make people give in more. Talk to yourself the way you would to a friend, then do the next small thing.
7. Secrets are heavy: A secret weighs on you every time it comes to mind, not only when you hide it. One safe person can share the weight.
9. If this, then that: Decide ahead of time with an if-then plan: “If this happens, then I will do that.” At 1 AM you only have to follow it.
10. Change the setting: Habits lean on their setting: the room, the device, the hour. Change the setting, and the cue gets weaker.
12. What getting better looks like: Getting better is growth with setbacks, across a whole life: health, home, purpose, and people. A streak is one part, not the whole picture.
13. Name the feeling: Urges often ride in on a feeling. Name it in a word or two, and it loses some of its grip. Then meet that feeling another way.
15. Move your body: Yes. A short burst of movement eases cravings for a while. When an urge starts, move first, then decide.
16. Thoughts are not orders: They are thoughts, not orders. Notice them, name them, and still choose. You do not have to argue with them or obey them.
19. Learn from your own log: Write it down, then look back. Once a week, ask what the log is telling you: when it is hard, what sets it off, and what helps.
20. Fewer fights, not more willpower: Not mostly. People with strong self-control fight temptation less, not more. Arrange your day so the fight happens less, and count the fights you skip.
21. Missing a day: No. A single missed day barely dents a new habit, but misses add up. The day after, come back in the smallest way.
23. Plan the empty hour: Do not wait to feel like it. Put a real, small activity in your hardest hour, and do it even if you do not feel like it.
28. Why groups help: Groups change who you spend time with, and that is one of the main ways they help. Start small: listen at one meeting, or ask one person to check in.

journal.book:
MY PLAYBOOK

Why I am doing this
- Being fully present with the people I love
- Clear mornings and steady energy
- Becoming someone I am proud of

My rule
I log slips instead of hiding them. A slip is data, not a reset.

If this, then that
If I am in bed late at night, then Get up and leave the room for 10 minutes. Water, stretch, tidy something. Then back to bed without my phone.
If I am lonely or low, then Text or call one person. A message counts. Or go somewhere with people around.
If I am bored or idle, then 10-minute walk outside, or 10 minutes on a hobby or project.
If I am stressed or anxious, then Move my body (walk, pushups), then write one sentence about what is stressing me.

If I slip
1. Log it in 30 seconds. No hiding.
2. One small action within the hour: water, step outside, or text someone.
3. No big decisions tonight, and no "I blew it" verdicts.
4. Tomorrow: check in as usual. Nothing resets. Ask what the trigger was and what to change.
5. If I want to, tell my safe person: "I slipped."

What I have learned
1. You do not need to feel ready: No. Mixed feelings are a normal part of change. Start with one small step, and let your own reasons carry it.
2. Urges are waves: An urge rises, peaks, and passes. You do not have to fight it or obey it. Notice it, breathe, and outlast this one.
3. Why one slip snowballs: The slip is not the biggest risk. The thought “I blew it, so why bother” is. Protect your confidence and do the next small thing.
4. Late and low: Tired and lonely both make porn look like a bigger reward than it is. Meet the need under the urge: sleep, or a real person.
5. Name the act, not yourself: Describe what you did, not who you are: “I slipped last night,” not “I am a failure.” Then protect your next good move.
6. Kindness after a slip: No. Kindness did not make people give in more. Talk to yourself the way you would to a friend, then do the next small thing.
7. Secrets are heavy: A secret weighs on you every time it comes to mind, not only when you hide it. One safe person can share the weight.
9. If this, then that: Decide ahead of time with an if-then plan: “If this happens, then I will do that.” At 1 AM you only have to follow it.
10. Change the setting: Habits lean on their setting: the room, the device, the hour. Change the setting, and the cue gets weaker.
12. What getting better looks like: Getting better is growth with setbacks, across a whole life: health, home, purpose, and people. A streak is one part, not the whole picture.
13. Name the feeling: Urges often ride in on a feeling. Name it in a word or two, and it loses some of its grip. Then meet that feeling another way.
15. Move your body: Yes. A short burst of movement eases cravings for a while. When an urge starts, move first, then decide.
16. Thoughts are not orders: They are thoughts, not orders. Notice them, name them, and still choose. You do not have to argue with them or obey them.
19. Learn from your own log: Write it down, then look back. Once a week, ask what the log is telling you: when it is hard, what sets it off, and what helps.
20. Fewer fights, not more willpower: Not mostly. People with strong self-control fight temptation less, not more. Arrange your day so the fight happens less, and count the fights you skip.
21. Missing a day: No. A single missed day barely dents a new habit, but misses add up. The day after, come back in the smallest way.
23. Plan the empty hour: Do not wait to feel like it. Put a real, small activity in your hardest hour, and do it even if you do not feel like it.
28. Why groups help: Groups change who you spend time with, and that is one of the main ways they help. Start small: listen at one meeting, or ask one person to check in.
